The World Systems Theory describes semi-periphery countries as intermediate in economic complexity and power between core countries (which have diversified, developed economies) and periphery countries (which often have economies centered on a single natural resource).  
Semi-periphery countries typically have some industrialization and more economic diversity than periphery nations but are not as dominant as core nations.  

Looking at the options:  
- (A) Strong central government — not specific to semi-periphery.  
- (B) Economy centralized around one natural resource — more typical of periphery countries.  
- (C) Diversified and developed economy — more characteristic of core countries.  
- (D) Small percentage of very high class individuals — not a defining feature of semi-periphery.  

None perfectly match the standard definition, but semi-periphery countries often have some economic diversification without being fully developed, so (C) is the closest among these, though it’s more strongly associated with core countries. However, in comparative terms, (C) is still the best match because semi-periphery countries have more diversified economies than periphery countries.  

Final answer: (C)
